articles.title: Reported attacks on ships near Strait of Hormuz hit a new weekly high
articles.summary: What to know about the Iran war today: The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations monitoring agency said at least 10 vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since last Sunday, a weekly high since war broke out in February, and 23 attacks were recorded since the start of the month, almost double the average. Yemen's foreign minister blasted Iran's offer to mediate the war between the internationally recognized government and the Iran-backed Houthi militant group. "When Iran's foreign minister and his officials offer 'mediation' in Yemen, they are offering to mediate a war ignited by the coup of the Houthi terrorist militia with their regime's backing," she said. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister. Yemeni foreign minister criticizes Iranian offer to mediate Houthi war Yemen's foreign minister is blasting Iran's offer to mediate the war between the internationally recognized government and the Iran-backed Houthi militant group. "When Iran's foreign minister and his officials offer 'mediation' in Yemen, they are offering to mediate a war ignited by the coup of the Houthi terrorist militia with their regime's backing, and prolonged by that regime's arming, financing, and training of the militia and its supply of missiles, drones, and experts," Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah Alzouba said as part of a lengthy statement . "Tehran has made itself a party to the war on Yemenis," she continued. "Instead of offering mediation, its regime should withdraw its hand and its weapons from Yemen, respect the sovereignty of states, and abide by international law and the principles of good neighborliness." Iran's foreign ministry on Friday rejected Saudi Arabia's accusation that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering to mediate between the two sides. The Houthis are backed financially and militarily by Iran, officials from the U.S. and Israel, as well as many regional analysts, have said for years . "The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group, told CBS News. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next." Iranian foreign minister meets with several Middle East counterparts at regional gathering Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, one of the leading members of past negotiations with the United States, met with a handful of his counterparts on Saturday at a gathering of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad. Among those he met was Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan even as Turkey is part of a trilateral cooperation agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which is coming under fire from the Iran-backed Houthi militia. The two sides discussed "the latest developments in Palestine and Yemen, emphasizing diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions," according to the Iranian government. "During the bilateral talks, FM Araghchi also reviewed the latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, briefing his Turkish counterpart on ongoing diplomatic trends and emphasizing Islamic cooperation to face shared regional challenges," the Iranian government said on X . Araghchi also met with foreign leaders from Egypt, which said Saturday it would defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks; Libya; Lebanon; and Algeria. Saudi strikes on Yemen kill 12, Iran-backed Houthis say Saudi strikes that began overnight have killed at least 12 people in Yemen, three of them children, Houthi media reported on Saturday. Saudi warplanes targeted "civilian homes" in Taiz governorate on Saturday, killing nine people and wounding 16, the Iran-backed group's news agency said, adding people were still trapped under the rubble. The agency had earlier reported overnight strikes in Dhamar province that killed three children and wounded 17 other people. It said the strikes were carried out "using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally." The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis has launched daily raids in Yemen backing the internationally recognized government in the country's long-running civil war. Saudis intercept 4 drones over country in recent hours The Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Iran-backed Houthis have intercepted four drones over Saudi territory in the last few hours, the group said. The drones were intercepted over the capital city of Riyadh, and in the Eastern, and Southern regions, according to the coalition. The Houthis have regularly launched drones and missiles at the Saudis every day for the last several weeks. The coalition announced overnight it had taken out two missile-launch platforms in the Saada Governorate, which is the northern-most region in Yemen and controlled by the Houthis. A missile launch one week ago hit King Khallid International Airport in Riyadh and killed 13 people. President Sisi says Egypt ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested" Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday said Egypt was ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested," as fighting flares between the kingdom and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. Since Yemen's war reignited in July, the Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last Saturday. The Houthis have also blockaded the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-flagged tankers, piling pressure on energy exports as Iran presses its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy, Sisi said Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, but added it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was "harmed or its security and stability threatened." "Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," he said. He added any deployment would require parliamentary approval and said he hoped lawmakers would convene in an emergency session to grant authorization "if it is requested of us." "I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sisi said. "We are speaking only about defense." Yemen's Houthis free 159 pro-government fighters under amnesty Yemen's Houthis on Saturday announced the release of 159 pro-government fighters under an amnesty announced after they seized swathes of land in a major offensive last month. The prisoners had "voluntarily surrendered themselves without fighting" as the Iran-backed group captured strategic positions along the Red Sea, Houthi official Abdelqader al-Murtada told a press conference in Sanaa. The Houthis' war with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government reignited in July after four years of calm, triggering attacks on Saudi oil shipments and other targets including airports. The International Committee of the Red Cross confirmed the unilateral release of 159 prisoners and said it had given support by organizing interviews and health checks, contacting families and helping arrange transport. Murtada said 323 prisoners were released under the amnesty last month after surrendering in Hodeidah governorate. Iran backs "political process" to resolve Saudi-Houthi conflict, foreign minister says Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran supports a "political process" to resolve the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a major attack one week ago. "We support an inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve the issue," Araghchi said in a speech at the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad. Araghchi repeated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides. Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh has not responded to Iran's overture. On Friday, Iran denied having anything to do with the Houthi attacks, after Saudi Arabia accused Tehran of encouraging the group's escalation. In his speech, Araghchi also said "either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together," adding Tehran was willing "to cooperate with all its brothers and neighbours to achieve the first option." The Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, which also includes armed groups in Iraq. Oil tanker reportedly hits mine in Strait of Hormuz Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps on Saturday said an oil tanker was on fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine in the waterway at the heart of the Middle East war. "A supertanker in violation of regulations, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil and attempting to pass illegally through the Strait of Hormuz, struck a mine, triggering an explosion and a fierce fire," the Iranian military said. The statement did not specify the exact location of the incident. "The tanker attempted to cross the strait with U.S. support... by deactivating all its tracking systems," the Guards added, also posting a video of a vessel in flames during the night. Ship attacked by RPG fired from small boat, British maritime agency said The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitoring agency reported on Saturday a second attack on a ship off the coast of Saudi Arabia, which took place a day early. In a post on social media , the UKMTO said: "The master of a tanker has reported being attacked by an RPG (rocket-propelled grenade) from a small boat, resulting in damage to the aft port quarter." Friday's attack is the second reported by the agency on that day off the coast of Al Jubayl in Saudi Arabia. "Crew are accounted for and reported safe," the UKMTO said, but the full extent of the damage and environmental impact were not known at the time of the report. Ship struck by "unknown projectile" off the coast of Saudi Arabia, maritime agency says A British maritime agency said Saturday it had received a report of a vessel struck on the Persian Gulf on Friday. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said the tanker had been struck by an "unknown projectile" off the coast of Saudi Arabia. "All crew are reported safe and have been evacuated. There is no reported environmental impact at the time of report," the statement added. The UKMTO had previously reported that October had become the busiest month for reported attacks on ships in the Strait Hormuz. Reported shipping attacks jump in Strait of Hormuz, British monitor says A British monitor says October has become the busiest month for reported attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since March, during the Iran war's opening months. That's as the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said it was "struggling to accurately report" the true number of attacks since most ships now refuse to report them. Still, UKMTO said 10 attacks were reported in the week ending Friday. One ship sank. Since early July, most attacks have occurred off Oman, where the U.S. military has been guiding vessels at risk of Iranian attack. There has been an uptick in attacks since President Trump late last month rejected a Tehran proposal to end the war and open the strait, though indirect negotiations have continued. 2 missiles strike airport in Yemen's port city of Aden, officials say Two missiles struck the airport in Yemen's port city of Aden on Friday night, police said, blaming Iran-backed Houthi rebels for the second such attack in less than a week. Police said no casualties were reported as fighting escalates in the latest front in the Iran war, one in which the rebels have attacked both neighboring Saudi Arabia and Yemen's internationally recognized government that's backed by the kingdom. A security official and a traffic controller told The Associated Press an area of the Aden airport that hosts a military unit aligned with the Saudi-backed government was hit. Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks Iran's foreign ministry on Friday rejected Saudi Arabia's accusation that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering to mediate between the two sides. "The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement, reiterating Tehran's offer to act as a bridge between the Houthis and Riyadh. Regardless of how involved Iran has been in Houthi attacks, the two groups have long held close ties . They were once a relatively marginal group within what Iran calls its Axis of Resistance — a loose alliance of anti-Israel, anti-U.S. militant groups that includes Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. "The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," said Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next." Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have killed about 20 people in the last several weeks, including 13 in one strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport last weekend. CBS/AFP Iran's president denies nuclear ambitions, says country ready for talks Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister. In his meeting with Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Pezeshkian also called for closer ties with Georgia, weeks after Tbilisi cut aviation links between the two countries following U.S. sanctions targeting Iranian airlines. The two met on the sidelines of a U.N. biodiversity summit in Armenia's capital, Yerevan. "Iran is not seeking nuclear weapons, and we consider the malicious propaganda against our country to be lies," Pezeshkian said, according to a statement from his office. "We have always been ready for dialogue. They think they can force us to surrender, but we will not bow to coercion," he added, calling U.S. sanctions against Tehran "unjustifiable and inhumane." Georgia's Civil Aviation Agency said in September it would comply with U.S. sanctions, while Kobakhidze insisted Tbilisi was not imposing its own bilateral sanctions on Tehran. Saudi-hosted Asian Cup soccer tournament remains on schedule despite Houthi attacks Asian Cup organizers insisted Friday the continental soccer championship set to be held in Saudi Arabia in early 2027 remains on track despite a wave of missile and drone attacks on the host country in recent days. The Saudi organizing committee issued a statement Friday saying it is continuing to coordinate closely with the Asian Football Confederation. The tournament is scheduled for Jan. 7 to Feb. 5. "Preparations across all organizational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services," Saudi organizers said. "The focus remains on delivering a world-class tournament experience for participating teams, fans and media from across Asia, while bringing the continent together through football." South Korea's Professional Footballers' Association had earlier expressed concerns following a series of attacks on the Asian Cup host country by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. "The continued military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that can never be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, head of the South Korean player union, said in a statement. "The safety of our national team, as well as all players participating in the Asian Cup, is a serious concern." At least 19 people, including foreigners, have been killed in more than a week of Houthi attacks targeting the Riyadh international airport, the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco and other aviation, oil and military facilities across the kingdom. Several sporting events have already been canceled or postponed in Saudi Arabia, including Netflix's Six Kings Slam tennis tournament; women's tennis' WTA Finals, which were moved to the U.S.; multiple matches for the Saudi soccer club Al-Nassr, which features Cristiano Ronaldo; and an Olympic qualifying event for BMX cycling. AP/CBS Attacks on Yemen government palace compound killed 5, officials say Attacks on the palace compound of Yemen's internationally recognized government Thursday killed at least five people and wounded more than a dozen others, government officials said. In a Facebook post late Thursday, Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said security guards and other employees at Maashiq palace in Yemen's southern port city of Aden were among the casualties. Aden has been the seat of Yemen's government since 2015. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they targeted a military operations headquarters associated with Saudi forces backing the government. Two of the missiles launched by the Houthis on Thursday struck near the headquarters of the Saudi-backed coalition forces in Aden, causing damage, a Yemeni government official said. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak to the media, said Friday the missiles landed near the compound used by the coalition in Buraiqah, a neighborhood west of the palace. No senior officials were there at the time of the attack, he said. Saudi-led coalition intercepts missiles and drones Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki announced a series of interceptions in successive X posts on Friday, saying Saudi forces had destroyed a ballistic missile, two cruise missiles and three drones over Saudi Arabia or the Red Sea. In a first tweet, Al-Maliki said coalition forces intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Yanbu. A second post announced the interception and destruction of two cruise missiles over the Red Sea. He then reported three drones had been intercepted and destroyed in Saudi Arabia's southern region and the Riyadh region. Iraq says Iran war has deprived it of $60 billion in oil export revenue Iraq has lost around $60 billion during the U.S.-Iran war, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Thursday, as the fighting has blocked or severely impeded a waterway crucial to its oil exports. OPEC member Iraq was producing about 4 million barrels of oil per day (bpd) before the conflict, and exporting about 3.5 million bpd – mostly carried by tankers out of the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's ongoing threat to vessels that fail to seek its permission to transit the strait has forced Iraq, which lacks sufficient storage capacity, to halt most production and fall back on limited exports via Syria and Turkey, by truck and pipeline respectively. Syria is set to provide an overland oil route to bypass the strait , the head of Syrian Petroleum Co. said last week. "Iraq has suffered losses estimated at around $60 billion during the recent war between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran," Hussein told his Italian counterpart in Rome, according to a statement from the Iraqi foreign ministry. After a heavy drop in production, Iraqi oil exports, which provide about 90% of the country's revenues, recovered modestly last month, reaching 2.6 million barrels per day between Sept. 1 and 21, according to the oil ministry. But at the same time, Iraq's foreign currency reserves have shrunk by $20 billion and consumer prices have risen sharply, plunging it into economic crisis. CBS/AFP Norwegian teen sentenced in U.K. to 20 years in prison for plotting murder for Iran-linked gang A Norwegian teenager convicted of traveling to Britain to carry out a contract killing on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison. Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot someone unknown to him for $28,000 last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield, in northern England, with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the U.K. In bodycam video released by police from the early hours of March 19, 2025, Natland emerges topless from his room and mimes a shooting gesture at a firearms officer before being slammed against a wall. It remains unknown who his intended target would have been. Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organized crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to London's counterterrorism police unit. Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to "contribute to murder" and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy. CBS/AP Iranian navy says a tanker is burning in the Gulf of Oman The Iranian navy said Friday that it had identified a tanker on fire in what it called a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz. The navy's public relations office said in a statement that military surveillance teams "discovered and identified a violating oil tanker that had caught fire in a prohibited area." The vessel had "switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman." The navy did not say how the tanker "caught fire" but added that "the consequences of uncoordinated movements along routes and in prohibited areas are the creation of insecurity and serious hazards for other vessels." At least three commercial vessels have been struck in the region in suspected Iranian attacks this week. Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves the region" The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves" the Middle East, an Iranian army official said Friday. "If the United States leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the countries of the region, and the global economy will improve," army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X . "If it does not leave, we will expel it." He did not elaborate on whether he was calling for a withdrawal of military forces sent during the current war, all U.S. military forces across the region, or military and non-military U.S. government personnel. Though there were credible reports earlier this month of oil exports from the Persian Gulf ramping back up to near pre-war levels , Iran and the U.S. continue offering conflicting narratives, with the Trump administration insisting the Strait of Hormuz is open, but Tehran claiming it is closed to all traffic unless Iranian authorities grant permission. Greek maritime risk firm Marisks warned Thursday that ships continue to face "indiscriminate attacks," even if they turn off their tracking systems, which many ships have been doing to avoid detection. Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to "ecocide" Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression" against his country. Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had taken a significant toll on nature that extended beyond national borders and required "international solutions." "What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian said at a nature summit in Armenia that was attended by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. Pezeshkian decried an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. in a recent interview with CBS News . "As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us, and they don't honor what they have put in writing. So, if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?" CBS/AFP White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment." A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon." Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics. CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran. Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit. Read more here . articles.title: Fast-moving Southern California wildfire burns homes and forces thousands to flee
articles.summary: A fast-moving wildfire in Southern California quickly consumed hundreds of acres and burned multiple homes after sparking in Orange County Friday, county officials said. The Norte Fire began around noon near a neighborhood in the San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano areas and by Friday evening had grown to 570 acres, the Orange County Fire Authority said. It’s one of several fires that have broken out since Thursday amid fierce Santa Ana winds affecting Southern California. “Our actions today will be to continue to attack the fire and work toward getting residents home as soon as it’s safe to so do,” Orange County Fire Authority Captain Greg Barta said Saturday morning in a video on X . Topography and weather conditions allowed the fire to grow rapidly, Orange County Division 3 Fire Chief Mark Backoff said in a video posted to social media Friday afternoon. Six homes have been destroyed or damaged by the fire, and two firefighters suffered “significant” injuries but are stable in area hospitals, fire officials said. Evacuation orders were issued for multiple areas in San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano, encompassing roughly 4,600 homes and 16,000 people, Orange County Fire Authority Chief TJ McGovern said. Officials asked residents to be patient as they evaluate when it will be safe to return home. Officials said progress had been made against the fire by the evening but warned conditions remained volatile. “A majority of the fire has been knocked down. However, we still have some homes that have been impacted here, and as you can see, the wind is still blowing pretty strong up here,” Orange County Fire Authority spokesperson Steve Concialdi said. The fire is now 5% contained as of Saturday morning. Crews’ objective is “keeping the fire within its current footprint,” McGovern said at a news conference Friday evening. Aerial footage from CNN affiliate KCBS showed multiple houses burning Friday afternoon. Resident Robert Morris called the sudden threat to homes “a wake-up call,” telling KCBS, “I’ve lived here since 1995, and this is the first time we’ve really ever had a fire in this area.” US Rep. Mike Levin, a Democrat whose district includes part of Orange County, said his family had to evacuate their San Juan Capistrano home while he attended an event nearby. Levin thanked firefighters for preventing greater damage from the fire and said “year-round wildfire season” has become the “new normal” for Southern California. Cars drive along Interstate 5 towards the Norte Fire in San Juan Capistrano, California, on October 16. Evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Orange County. - Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images Orange County sheriff’s deputies were going door to door in areas under evacuation order, telling people to leave for their safety, Sgt. Lizbeth Gwisdalla, a spokesperson for the sheriff’s department, told CNN. Ten schools were dismissed early “out of an abundance of caution” and sports and after-school programs were canceled, Capistrano Unified School District announced . Wind gusts in the area reached 25 mph Friday afternoon and remained elevated into the evening. The Santa Ana winds had eased to gusts of 17 mph by Saturday and are expected to diminish later in the weekend. “We’re going to be here for a number of days,” Concialdi said of the ongoing danger, stressing the need to guard against new fires that could erupt from embers blown by the strong Santa Ana winds. Fires spark across Southern California Several fires have broken out since Santa Ana winds began Thursday, forcing evacuations in other areas of Southern California. In Malibu, more than 7,000 structures were in areas under evacuation orders or warnings on Friday because of the Bryson Fire, which has burned roughly 150 acres and is 52% contained since starting Thursday evening, a Los Angeles County Fire spokesperson told CNN, estimating the number of people under evacuation orders to be in the hundreds. Crews make a stand in front of the Bryson Fire in Malibu, California, on Thursday, Oct. 15. - Jae C. Hong/AP Crews made “great progress” against the fire overnight, Los Angeles County Fire Chief Anthony Marrone said during a news conference Friday morning. At least one firefighter had “minor injuries” and was taken to the hospital, he said. The chief did not provide additional details except to say, “They’ve been on the line all night, so minor injuries are expected.” The fire is still threatening more than 100 structures in the area, but no damages have been reported. “But obviously, if the winds kick up later this afternoon and we were to lose containment of the fire, a larger area could be affected and under threat,” the chief said. Over 400 firefighters and more than 75 “ground and aerial resources” are committed to the Bryson Fire, he said. Another wildfire to the south has burned more than 3,000 acres near the Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton since igniting Thursday afternoon, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection ( Cal Fire ). The Henderson Fire forced a temporary evacuation order for one area of the base Thursday and the closure of a nearby portion of Interstate 5 in San Diego County, the Marine Corps said in a statement Friday. Smoke affected visibility along both sides of the highway Friday afternoon, the California Highway Patrol said. The fire is 35% contained as of Saturday morning, according to Cal Fire . The Camp Pendleton Fire Department and Cal Fire continue to actively fight the fire, but it was burning “in a remote section” of the base and there were no active threats to personnel or facilities, the Marine Corps statement Friday said. The dangerous fire conditions in Southern California have also prompted utility companies to temporarily shut off power for tens of thousands over concerns that equipment could spark fires. This story has been updated with additional information. Meteorologist Chris Dolce and CNN’s Kate S. Petersen and Isa Mudannayake contributed to this report. articles.title: Trump says neither he or Musk are to blame for Ukraine drone issues
articles.summary: Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump. "Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored." Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory. "Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems." "Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity." Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating" Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions. Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia. "Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters. "President Trump has been clear that he wants to see this brutal war come to an end. As talks continue, this Act provides the President with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News on Saturday in response to a question about lifting the sanctions. "Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing U.S. efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The President retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time if he determines that doing so would advance national interests." Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire. In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said. On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted : "Time for Zelensky to go." articles.title: French police clash with protesters as tens of thousands rally over cost of living
articles.summary: By Janis Laizans, STAMOS PROUSALIS and Yann Tessier PARIS, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Violent clashes erupted between police and protesters across France on Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of people protested against rising costs and declining public services in some of the country's most destructive unrest in years. The Interior Ministry said at least 272 people had been arrested after violent ‌incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Toulouse in the southwest, Angers in the west and Lyon in east-central France. Belgium, Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests ‌on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government  would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on ​the "far-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year. "To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X. The CGT union told Agence France-Presse news agency that 800,000 people across France had taken part in Saturday's protests. The Interior Ministry did not give an estimate, and the CGT did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and ‌clash with the police. "We are fighting because the cost of living is ⁠too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris. TEAR GAS, FIRE AND LOOTING In some parts of Paris, police ⁠occasionally fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and  goggles to protect against tear gas. By late afternoon, protesters reached prominent landmarks in central Paris, including the Champs-Elysees, Concorde and La Madeleine, which had been excluded from the authorised demonstration. On Saturday evening, as the protests wound down, protesters set ablaze objects including at least one car. Some tourists at a fashionable department ​store ​near the Paris opera were seen spluttering when they were caught in clouds of tear gas, and shops nearby ​were hastily shuttered. Windows of many shops and restaurants in the capital were smashed, ‌and cars and trash cans were set on fire. In Lyon, protesters torched the tourist office. In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalised and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the government. In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible. In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down. In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling ‌one of the worst affordability crises in Europe. In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into ​disorder, with police clearing the central Cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannon to try to ​disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported. FRENCH ​POLICE RESPONSE UNDER SCRUTINY The protests in France began last month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved ‌into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards. In Paris on ​Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the ​Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron's previous term in office. Macron, who urged calm on Friday, is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy. France's efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades. Police tactics have drawn criticism following ​injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up ‌a stun grenade. Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured in previous protests. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence. (Reporting ​by Janis Laizans, Stamos Prousalis, Yann Tessier, Clotaire Achi, Dominique Vidalon, Makini Brice and Sybille de La Hamaide in Paris, Stephane Mahe in Nantes, Petra Wischgoll in Strasbourg, Marc ​Leras in Marseille. Writing by Sybille de La Hamaide. Editing by Hugh Lawson, Mark Potter and Timothy Heritage) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/students-trade-unions-yellow-vests-050603763.html

articles.title: Katie Zacharia praises Trump as ‘kind, wonderful, gracious’ after White House exit
articles.summary: President Trump's embattled new press secretary Katie Zacharia was forced out Friday after less than a week on the job. Zacharia confirmed widespread reports that Trump had let her go in a post on X just after 9 p.m. ET Friday, alongside a photo of the two of them in the Oval Office. “President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man,” she wrote. “I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him.” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung told CNN in a statement that Zacharia "will continue to support the President as she transitions to a new role." Zacharia is the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in U.S. history. Her five days on the job fell well short of Anthony Scaramucci’s 11 days as Trump’s communications director in 2017. Trump is unlikely to name a new press secretary anytime soon, two sources familiar with his thinking told NBC News . Earlier Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia was on her way out, telling reporters that he had asked Zacharia to "reconsider" whether she "need[s] this." "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy and I don't think you could ever be happy in this job,'" Trump said. Asked if he was planning to "fire" Zacharia, the president said no. But, he added, "I want her to have a good life. I don't want [her] to have a life like she's led in the last three days. She is being brutalized by the media." Around the same time, multiple outlets reported that Zacharia had already been let go. Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had "fired" Zacharia. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role, and CBS News, Politico and the Washington Post published similar reports. Zacharia was in the middle of an interview with the Wall Street Journal at her West Wing desk shortly before 1 p.m. Friday when she was called away, the Journal reported . She had just told the reporters, “There are no staffing changes that are happening.” Senior Trump adviser Jason Miller then knocked on her door and said Vice President JD Vance wanted to talk. “JD wanted to chat with us real quick,” Miller said, according to the Journal. Zacharia left and never returned to the interview. Trump: "I told Katie that in my opinion she was treated very very unfairly by the news. Let's call it the fake news. I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this.' We're talking about doing something. I want her to have a good life. She's being brutalized by the… pic.twitter.com/Ivkk5imCjS — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 16, 2026 The president announced on Friday, Oct. 9, that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August. Zacharia started at the White House on Monday and gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than Trump's agenda. In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State. In media appearances, Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia." Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China." In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper.  "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One.  And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question." Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia looks on as President Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time. On Thursday, Zacharia confirmed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China." On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer." White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added. Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law." "I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice,"  she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'" On Thursday night, Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her halting explanation . "Why not just say, 'I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn't pass it'?" Hannity asked. "Why get into this long drawn-out thing about the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?" "When I moved back to the United States, I didn't retake the bar," Zacharia said. "I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law." Hours before she was forced out, Zacharia told “Fox & Friends” on Friday that no one had asked whether she passed the bar before she was hired. “Those questions weren’t asked,” she said. “I’m being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel,” according to The Hill . What happened in Zacharia's first briefing? White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the  Briefing Room on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Zacharia's first briefing lasted 15 minutes, most of which was taken up by her opening statement. "I am so honored to work for President Trump and the American people as the new White House press secretary," Zacharia told reporters in the Briefing Room. "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time." She took questions from three news outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — before ending the briefing. Asked what she planned to do as press secretary, Zacharia said, "I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was getting to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people." In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump said Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on X . Who is Katie Zacharia? President Donald Trump and Katie Zacharia. Katie Zacharia/X The 42-year-old California native and mother of four left her role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social, to join the White House. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn profile . She was best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol." Zacharia first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California with her husband and their four young children. During Tuesday's briefing, she was asked about juggling the competing roles of being a mother and White House press secretary. "The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable," Zacharia said, before confusing her spouse with her boss. "So my president — excuse me, my husband — is out here." Zacharia then praised Trump as the "most family-friendly president we've ever had" and said her family will be moving from California to Washington, D.C., soon. CNN reported on Friday that Zacharia's "selection came about quickly" and that she "was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position." In a New York Post column in February , Zacharia recounted a clash with liberal patrons of her "local cardio kickboxing gym" that ended with the gym owner asking her not to wear her red "Team Trump 2024" hat to exercise class. "I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent." articles.title: Police identify teenage gunman, teacher and 5-year-old killed in Oregon shooting
articles.summary: A teacher and one of the three children who were killed in Thursday's mass shooting at a Bend, Ore., elementary school were identified on Friday during a press conference in which authorities provided additional details about the incident. The 16-year-old suspect, who was killed by a community member within minutes of opening fire at the school, was also identified. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Friday that Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old student, and Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, were among the four victims in a special education classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School. In a statement, Lambert's family described her as a native central Oregonian who grew up in Bend and had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. "Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in," the statement continued.  "Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher. … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. … She was funny and opinionated and she lit up the room." Megan Lambert, 25, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., was killed in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed in Thursday's shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore. Bend Police Department The shooter was identified as Griffin J. John II. He was a former student at the school who had received special ed services, according to Bend-La Pine School Superintendent Steven Cook. The two other children killed, both boys, were 8 and 11. Their families asked police not to release their names. A 7-year-old girl who received lifesaving care at the scene was in serious but stable condition at Oregon Health & Science University, police said. A 54-year-old teacher, Becky Drury of Bend, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and was being treated at St. Charles Bend. Her family allowed police to release her name. Becky Drury, 54, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, was injured in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department According to a Facebook post from her mother-in-law, Drury has already had surgery to repair significant damage to her left arm and will need more surgeries in the future. She also suffered injuries to her right hand, but none of her wounds are believed to be life-threatening. "The good news is she will be ok and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives," the post read. Police declined to confirm the name of the bystander who killed John, but he has been identified by multiple news outlets as Kaylub Giamanco, a lifelong Bend resident with two young daughters at the school. Police have described him only as a 36-year-old man. "He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support," Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, said while reading a prepared statement to reporters outside her son's home near the school. "I don't think we can underestimate or underappreciate [his] courage," Krantz said Friday, referring to Giamanco's decision to intervene. "When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. And the quick thinking to … follow someone into the school is incredible, and undoubtedly saved people." Other than John's past association with the school, police did not share any information on the potential motive behind the shooting. "Everyone wants to know why, including us," Krantz said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it." Krantz said John used a Maverick 88 12-gauge pump-action shotgun in the shooting. He declined to comment on where he acquired the gun. Law enforcement sources told NBC News and CBS News that John’s mother bought the shotgun around his birthday in August. Police said Friday that how he got the weapon and ammunition remains part of the active investigation. How the shooting unfolded Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Friday. AP Photo/Haven Daley Krantz provided new details about what happened in the chaotic few minutes from when John first opened fire outside the school to when he was killed. According to Krantz, John approached the school at approximately 12:58 p.m. on foot before throwing his gun over an exterior fence and climbing onto the school's property. A driver in a red pickup truck spotted John and "verbally confronted" him from inside their vehicle. John fired at least three rounds at the truck before heading inside. The driver, who was unhurt, quickly called 911 to alert police. John then walked around the outside of the school and fired multiple rounds into the glass panes of an exterior door to gain access to the school. He then turned left into a special education classroom and immediately began firing. In total, John fired as many as 15 rounds, Krantz said. Giamanco, who had seen John fire at the pickup truck, parked his car in the school parking lot, grabbed his pistol and began following John's path into the school. As he entered through the shot-out doors, Giamanco found a teacher involved in a physical altercation with John. He fired several rounds from his pistol, striking John multiple times. Before Giamanco arrived, a teacher in the classroom threw her cell phone at John, then tackled him and fought to take the gun from him, police said. She was not injured. Officers arrived at the scene within three minutes of the first 911 call. "Seconds later, officers reported the suspect had been shot and killed, possibly by a bystander," police wrote in an incident report on Thursday. Officers then cleared the school, and all students and staff were transported to a nearby church for reunification with families and guardians. According to Krantz, John was carrying an additional 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. No other students other than the three who were killed and the one who was injured were in the classroom at the time, Krantz said. There was no School Resource Officer present at the school. Investigators have searched John’s home and plan to keep control of the school until at least Tuesday to finish collecting evidence, police said. They are asking anyone with video of a teenage boy in black clothing and a black backpack near Third Street, Brosterhous Road or the school between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. Thursday to submit it. The FBI has set up a tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI and fbi.gov/silverrailschool . 'They're babies' People leave a family reunification area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline Witnesses described hearing gunshots and seeing police swarm the school. "I heard what I thought was gunshots," Erin Johnson, who was visiting her parents next door to the school, told Oregon Public Broadcasting on Thursday. "Then my neighbor began to scream shortly thereafter — her kids go to school there, at Silver Rail. Then I heard the police coming in." She added: "It's heartbreaking. I don't know any details right now about who was injured. But they're babies." Krista Johnson told OregonLive that she saw police swarm the school. "So many people stopping what they were doing," she said Thursday. "I knew that something had happened." Angela Nuchols told the Bend Source that she and her husband had dressed their 8-year-old daughter up for picture day before school, then raced to Silver Rail after hearing about the shooting. "It was crawling with police officers from all over the county," she said. "You've got guys in tactical gear, rifles. You're just scared to death wondering, is your child okay? You don't know." They were later reunited with their daughter. "It was like the worst three hours of our lives," Nuchols said. Thousands attended a vigil at Bend's Drake Park on Thursday night, many carrying candles, flowers and stuffed toys. “There is power and love in this park tonight,” Gov. Tina Kotek said at the vigil, "On behalf of everyone who lives in Oregon, I am so sorry for what you are experiencing today. No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day." Free counseling is being offered to anyone in the community who may need help dealing the emotional weight of the tragedy. As of Friday afternoon, close to 200 people had already utilized those services, according to Deschutes County Health Services Director Mary Harris. The Bend Education Association, which represents 1,000 educators in the city, released a statement emphasizing the work that will be needed to ensure that every student and teacher affected by the shooting has the support that they need. "When violence happens in one of our schools, it reaches far beyond that building," the group's president, Sarah Barclay, wrote on social media. "It affects our families, our colleagues, and communities across our country. Every student and every person who works in our schools deserves to be safe." articles.title: Trump's decision to waive Russia sanctions sparks bipartisan outrage
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia . Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia's Vladimir Putin . Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3. “Beyond irresponsible,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on social media, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the sanctions that were supposed to take effect Sunday targeting Russian's economy could be revived. “What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?” Tillis said. “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.” Tillis said that if Trump wants to actually bring down energy prices, he should resolve the Iran war , which is largely blamed for the spike at the pump, and “not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.” Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said “Lindsey would be appalled,” referring to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a statement that “by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier.” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Trump is “thumbing his nose” at Congress and “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.” She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course. Trump's actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia's ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on. Zelenskyy, who has endured a rocky relationship with Trump but stayed close to the U.S. lawmakers, urged supporters to speak out on behalf of the sanctions. The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate are on recess until after Election Day. Trump said he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns. It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump’s moves until lawmakers return to Washington. Skeptics in Congress warned Trump would not follow the law It took almost a year for Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package. It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as way to halt the flow of funds fueling Putin's four-year war against Ukraine. But even as Zelenskyy had watched from the visitor gallery as the Senate advanced the package after Graham's death, skeptics in Congress warned Trump would be unlikely to follow the bill once he had signed it into law a month ago. Last week, a bipartisan group of senators urged the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on Russia, particularly the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions. The senators noted that the bulk of the new law's provisions were to be effective Sunday. Instead, Trump soon announced the diesel deal with Putin, saying that Russia had agreed to supply tons of fuel to the U.S., where gas prices have skyrocketed in some areas and voters saying affordability issues are a top concern. Outraged lawmakers have pledged to stop the Trump-Putin deal. New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee who had led opposition to the Graham bill — warning that Trump would flout the law — introduced legislation Friday that would block Trump's diesel deal with Putin. “At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine," Meeks said in a statement. He called the deal “corrupt” and said it “goes against everything the United States stands for.” On Saturday, he said that "Congress is not helpless" and must act. Graham's legacy on the line Graham's sister, Darline Graham of South Carolina, helped ensure Senate passage of the bill, once she was appointed by the state's governor to fill her brother's seat. She is now running against Democrat Annie Andrews in a tight race. Trump is expected in the state next week to rally voters. “Look, the president and I share the same goal, which is to end the war, to get gas and diesel prices down, and the sanctions bill is one of the tools he can use to do that,” Darline Graham said at a campaign stop Saturday. “It’s up to him whether or not he chooses to use it. Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she said, “because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.” Like her brother, who often publicly parted ways with the president, Darline Graham said she and Trump can have their differences. “I am proud of it to help get across the finish line. It meant a lot to Lindsey,” she said. “But you know, like Lindsey, he disagreed with the president sometimes they had that relationship where they could agree to disagree sometimes. And I think that just happens." __ Associated Press writers Meg Kinnard in Mount Pleasant, S.C., and Kevin Freking and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report. articles.title: Judge denies gag order request in Cornell sex assault civil case
articles.summary: A New York judge on Friday rejected a request to impose a gag order in the civil case brought by a former Cornell University student who alleged she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024, calling the request a "'side show' meant to muddy the waters and distract from the merits of the claims and defenses involved in this case." Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond said the public statements made by Jane Doe's attorney that one of the men named in the civil lawsuit used to justify the request "express nothing more than [his] opinions." Cornell president defends response to Jane Doe allegations in heated faculty meeting "Expressing opinions on the case or reporting on how the litigation has impacted clients cannot alone serve as a factual basis for limiting an individual's First Amendment rights," Judge Perry-Bond wrote. "While the Court agrees that [he] should not make statements that certain parties spoliated evidence, especially where, as here, no discovery has yet to take place, those isolated statements, without more, are insufficient to show the serious risk of prejudice required by precedent and the United States Constitution." The judge encouraged the attorneys in the case to work together to prevent their clients from facing threats, harassment, and doxing. "The Court believes that given the notoriety of doxing related to this case, it would serve all parties' interests to work together to ensure their clients and others may be safeguarded, to the extent possible, from being inundated with threats or harassment from malicious outside actors," she wrote. Angelina Katsanis/Reuters - PHOTO: Cornell University in Ithaca, New York Perry-Bond also rebuked the lawyer who requested the gag order for including in a court filing an email exchange with an attorney for one of the other men. "The Court will not tolerate its docket being used to generate media controversy, and this Court does not tolerate attorneys, especially attorneys who are not even involved in this case, engaging in mudslinging," she wrote. The attorneys requesting the gag order had asked for "narrowly tailored restrictions" that would prevent lawyers and parties in the civil case from commenting on the allegations outside of court, arguing in their motion that a gag order would limit "possible juror prejudice" and prevent the potential release of sensitive information that could lead to " threats, doxing, intimidation, and extrajudicial contact." In a statement responding to the motion response, an attorney for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, argued that the attorney for one of the men "has tried to rebut the claims in this case by engaging in a wholesale leaking of confidential documents, giving interviews calling Ms. Doe's story into question and calling her lawsuit immoral. These attempts to shift the narrative have not been successful." Accused Cornell University student asks for gag order A then-undergraduate student identified only as Jane Doe made a complaint to campus police in November 2024, three weeks after the alleged incident occurred, that she had been sexually assaulted by a group of men at the Chi Phi fraternity house. She filed a civil suit against seven men and the university alleging that she had been drugged and raped. The men denied all of the allegations. The university has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies." The school said it conducted a "thorough" Title IX investigation and "issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. This week, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff announced that all parties and social events at fraternity houses are suspended for the rest of year while the university considers whether fraternity life can continue at the Ivy League school. "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," Kotlikoff said Tuesday. No criminal charges have been filed, but an investigation by the New York attorney general is ongoing. The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/US/judge-denies-gag-order-request-cornell-sex-assault/story?id=137338006
